records.title: Show HN: Agentic Identity Broker, OAuth Delegation for AI Agents
records.author: jbspeakr
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I’m Jan. I am co-author of the Agentic Identity Broker (AIB), an MIT-licensed OAuth2 broker in the Zalando Incubator, that lets a user give an AI agent scoped, revocable access to MCP services.

The broker solves three major challenges that are especially relevant in corporate environments: (A) Enable users to delegate workloads to agents without providing the agents all the user’s tokens. (B) Connect fragmented identity and authorization systems. (C) Centralize tool approvals and audit logging.

We built AIB to fill an infrastructure gap in our own agent platform. At this moment in time, IETF working groups are still finalizing standards for agent identity, and vendors are still turning the necessary infrastructure into off-the-shelf products. We needed that infrastructure today.

How it works: the user consents once per agent and service. The broker stores the third-party tokens encrypted. At request time a gateway (e.g. Agentgateway) does RFC 8693 token exchange. Agents never see user tokens and MCP servers only implement tools and don’t need to care about all the OAuth 2.1 plumbing.

AIB is v0.1 and runs in production, bringing together hundreds of our agents with dozens of internal and external MCP servers.

To try it locally: clone the repo, run "just compose-up-detached".

The current features focus on on-behalf-of (OBO) use cases, where human actors delegate to agents. Next we are looking to also support headless agents, where agents are invoked by machines. Intent-based authorization is yet another package on our roadmap. If you’ve built either, or have feedback on the UI/UX, I’d like to hear from you!

records.title: Show HN: HackerRepos – HackerTube for repos mentioned on HN
records.author: mmvvaa
records.storyText:
Karpathy posted hackertube.org 5 days ago, and mentioned that it took him 2 hours to build. A day after another fellow posted hackerbooks.org https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50326821, and made it to the top of HN. Some hours after someone else made it to the top of HN with the same for wikis: https://wikihack.netlify.app/ I found particularly interesting the "Trends" section on https://hackerbooks.org/

That night, I set out to build something similar but for Repos.

So I built https://HackerRepos.fyi. There are 57,316 repositories and 667,508 mentions indexed.

I originally made three main sections: Top of all time, Most Recommended, and Trends - per HackerBooks inspiration.

It looked/felt good, so I wanted to take it further.

I am a big fan of https://github.com/trending, and frequent it often, looking for inspiration. So I built the "Trending now section" https://hackerrepos.fyi/#/trending section. Trending now gives in a quick colour-coded sentiment snapshot of the repos trending on HN, using a grid/map in the style of https://finviz.com/.

When you click on a repo, it gives you a summary of the chatter, a colour-coder tag (Favorable, Critical, Debated, Informational), a graph of the mentions over time and the comments below the graph.

I also added a section on every repo called "Where it’s used", to showcase real world use cases. I realized populating this section could be costly, so I placed it behind a paywall for those that care for it. Pro users can click "Find real-world uses", and the app goes and finds a real-world use case.

I am working on a few other features I want to ship, but they are not ready yet. For example, I want to build a reverse product-to-stack exploration feature, where a user could enter or describe a product, and the app could provide a set of stacks to fit it, and perhaps, supporting comments. Also, I want to build task-based comparisons. I have a task, and I am debating between some repos to use. I could describe the task and enter the repos I have in mind to solve for the task, and have the app suggest the better one.

But I am glad I stopped and I am posting this now, because it has been a long time since I have finally managed to actually ship something from start to finish. I have a folder full of projects I started and did not ship. As I was struggling with this yesterday, whether I should make this public now or keep fiddling with it, I went to Mass and the gospel was Luke 14:25-33. The following part struck me:

"And indeed, which of you here, intending to build a tower, would not first sit down and work out the cost to see if he had enough to complete it? Otherwise, if he laid the foundation and then found himself unable to finish the work, anyone who saw it would start making fun of him and saying, Here is someone who started to build and was unable to finish."

So here it is. I finished this little tower. I hope you enjoy it, find it helpful, and if you care for it, sponsor it.

records.title: Show HN: Overhead – the planes overhead, painted on an e-ink frame
records.author: xDaftTurtle
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

I've been fascinated by aviation for some time now. Inspired by Fugleramme, I wanted a framed print of a cluster of aircraft over my house or a busy airport. So I built Overhead. (Photos in the README)

The hero photo shows planes departing and landing in Changi, Singapore.

How it works

Flight data for a location is gathered from adsb.lol and adsb.fi as a fallback. (you can also point it to your own ADS-B receiver).

The photo of the exact aircraft is gathered from planespotters.net and the photographer is credited on the page.

The photo is then handed to an AI image gen service via fal.ai using your own key.

It's then cut out and packed into a cluster on the page with packers adapted from Fugleramme.

It costs about US$0.04 a painting but images are painted once and kept for the next time that aircraft is seen.

You can also choose to only show photos.

This widget is built on my open source, self-hosted e-ink platform, Tesserae. It's a one click install from the widget catalog.

I'm looking for feedback and contributors.

https://github.com/arnegiacomo/fugleramme https://github.com/dmellok/tesserae

records.author: jomon003
records.storyText:
Glad to showcase SKI (https://justski.it) , a voice-first coding harness.

It supports multiple agents from different providers, just like conductor used to. You can run claude code, codex, antigravity etc. You can also add multiple subscriptions of Claude code or others, which will automatically switch when the limits are hit so that you can continue working on projects seamlessly

Voice first - You can talk to it, and it will talk back and keep you updated on tasks and status. You could also ask it to speak only when needed and it will adapt. (It doesn't read out the code line by line, unless you specifically ask it to). It is multilingual and supports 80+ languages. It can automatically convert the audio in your language to English for the models to work on. There is a optional review window if you need to verify it before sending to the agents.

Chain reactions: Maybe you need one agent to do a task, and then hand it over to the next agent. We call it chain. And you can just do it using voice easily in SKI.

Lives in notch (can be hidden behind notch as well, but also has a bigger UI like conductor)

Different voice for different sessions: Distinguish projects by voice.

Can take screenshots if you ask it to (will show flash)

One agent for all - Experimental feature where a single agent manages multiple sessions by voice, routing your requests on its own and keeping track of tasks across different sessions.

UI pop ups for things that need your attention - When in notch, agents will pop up options and explain what each options are, when they need an input from you. For instance, if there are 3 options for some task, the UI will show the 3 tasks as a floating window, which you can either click or choose by voice. Agents will also explain by voice if needed.

Floating taskbar like a widget - Floats when enabled, showing all tasks in different sessions and different agents, along with current progress and step. Can give voice inputs by just clicking on them and talking.

Loops - available for all agents as a harness tool

Computer use - Stays in notch and does without interfering your work.

Git integrated: Can create sessions from PR, merge, see comments etc. All by voice, text and UI buttons. Also custom branch names with configurable prefix.

Pricing: Text usage - Unlimited, free forever, No limits Voice: Free 300 credits per month.

records.title: Show HN: Grid – A Hold'em arena where your AI agent plays your strategy (Beta)
records.author: taelimoh
records.storyText:
Hi HN, my friend's team and I have been building a game called GRID, a dog poker game with an AI twist.

Under the cute dog graphics, GRID is an arena where LLMs compete, with no-limit hold’em as the medium. You duke it out as a strategist, vibe coder, and bot maker.

Why: models get compared on benchmarks all the time, but rarely as my agent against yours in its truest form. GRID is our attempt at creating that arena, because we believe this type of game will exist in the future, as AI becomes as common a tool as the browser.

How it works:

* Paste a prompt and an MCP config into Claude Code, Codex or any MCP client. The agent waits for its turn and sends actions back through tool calls.

* The strategy is text written in the game, up to 6,000 characters. We thought it’d be cool to have a preset, “Play like Elon”, to show you what you can do.

* You can change the strategy any time, and it applies from the next action. You can even ask your AI to change it for you, based on what it learns about its opponents’ strategies from the match history.

* Free beta. Play chips only. We just opened up the game today and are gathering data on how to steer this ship next.

Rough edges:

* MCP can be finicky, especially if you refresh your browser while in a match. If this happens and you can’t get your agent to connect, wait 5 min and retry | log out using the settings button at the top left and log back in. Stability is currently our top priority.

* MCP also uses a lot of tokens, more than the game should, because every tool call costs tokens. We plan to overhaul this with a new connection type in a future version so it’s much more efficient.

* There’s a built-in local model for folks who don’t want to use their own AI. It plays basic hold’em OK but struggles to follow written strategies. If you want to try it, I’d recommend leaving your strategy blank. Sadly, it plays best with no instructions.

* House bots fill empty seats. We made this choice so matches happen even when only a few people are online.

Honestly, I’m most curious how you’d write a strategy that holds up against everyone else’s agents. And if MCP setup breaks on you, please tell me. We'll be in the thread as long as possible.

records.title: Show HN: Botel – always reachable agents you pay for only while they're working
records.author: 4ver
records.storyText:
I built a pay-as-you-go two star hotel for bots that you’re only charged for while it’s active. Typically wakes in under a second, runs on a vm, and costs very little while it’s paused.

In my free time I’ve been building a firecracker based vm orchestration platform. In order to dogfood the thing I put together a place to run agent harnesses (openclaw etc) on machines but only pay for them when they are in use. What started as a demo has grown legs into a more unique product than the platform.

Botel has prebaked templates for each harness, with a daemon of mine running beside it monitoring the harness’ activity. It communicates out to the host over a link-local self api; instructing when to pause or wake next based on stored schedules. With a proxy in front to wake on http. The harnesses are preconfigured to point to my llm gateway that proxies through to openrouter.

One of the biggest struggles while building it was preventing claude from going off the rails with hotel metaphors in the ui. Once it sees a joke it really strangles the hell out of it.

A more real ;) awkward part is that the harnesses don’t expose exactly what I needed in order to detect activity. I'm still struggling with how to handle the fact that background job can be short or long lived (http/dev servers etc). I’m hoping to propose changes to hermes, openclaw, and dsh soon for a consistent way to know what kind of a job is running with annotated lifecycle hooks.

Some of the nicest things about the bot hotel are:

- You get a proper linux vm with sudo, so you can ssh in, scp, or run docker.

- You can ask the agent to expose something publicly or privately (behind your login). A port gets a unique hostname/url. Those endpoints also wake the vm. So you could build and host a little app or self host something.

- Guided telegram setup. It’s pretty awkward in general/my setup hopefully takes some of the edge off.

A friend of mine who built a website for his local orienteering club has used this to make it easy for peoge on the committee to update news and events. All in all it should cost something like 40 cents a month to run so long as the club members don’t get too friendly with the agent.

If you’re interested, give the thing a spin. The first 50 signups get $2 credit. Price is pretty low at 3c per GB of ram per hour awake, plus a few cents per GB-month asleep. You use credit for inference or byok.

Let me know how you get on and whether you have any ideas or requests for it. Thx!

records.title: Show HN: Thinker – Trim context and cache knowledge to extend agent usage limits
records.author: yoavshmariahu
records.storyText:
I’ve been doing a lot of solo development lately and found myself hitting Claude token limits halfway through the week constantly. Even with a Max plan, I’d have to switch over to Codex or Cursor, and it would be a bit difficult to get used to the nuances of each harness.

It’s still a problem for me, but I finally built Thinker to save me some tokens and help me get a bit more out of my coding agent subscriptions.

I started off a bit in the dark about how token billing works, and had to dig deeper to figure out what workflows ended up hurting my budget the most. By far, it was large context windows. Claude tries to help out on costs by offering prompt caching - which is sort of a bandage on the bigger problem: context bloat.

I find that my context window gets bloated with unneeded tokens in two main ways:

Tool outputs from subtasks that are long finished. File reads, Bash commands, MCP outputs, etc. Main idea is that the model finished the work but carries the weight of it for every subsequent call - translating to wasted token usage. CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md getting way too big. Lots of content gets dumped into these files as your agents work in your repo. I found that it’s not clear what is actually useful to be included there. Every token here counts, because it will be paid for in every session, and its cost scales linearly with the duration of your session.

Thinker addresses both of these issues. We have a proxy that wires in between your harness and model to cut out old context that we determine is no longer needed for your current task. Based on the provider you’re using, we determine the right time to batch enough context to cut that justifies the cache re-write cost, which gets paid off after X subsequent calls.

We also analyze your sessions and figure out which parts of your instruction files don’t really get used - and send you suggestions to cut or compress those sections. Thinker will kick off a subagent to do that work for you and open a PR you can review.

Finally, we use your sessions to record knowledge notes by distilling your sessions with a cheap model (Haiku, Luna). These notes are then served at prompt time via a cross-encoder, also on your machine, that decides whether a note is relevant to the user’s prompt.

Here are some data points to show how exactly Thinker saves you coding agent costs: https://thinker.sh/see-the-data

If you’re hitting problems at all with usage limits, it’d be great to hear how you’ve been trying to mitigate it.

Our open-source repo here (MIT License): https://github.com/yoavshmariahu/thinker

records.title: Show HN: Repairer – close the breach when a Linux flaw goes public
records.author: jaekwon
records.storyText:
As we've seen with the Ubuntu critical CVE-2026-98432 (CVSS 9.8), AI-dicovered zero day exploit are being reported at an exponential rate and we don't have the process for dealing with the flood of exploits in real time.

What we need is an AI-based system for autopatching systems based on real time information. The vendor's fix can take days or weeks to be out (is the Ubuntu thing patched yet?) and meanwhile the grid is vulnerable to exploitation, especially AI worms.

Repairer is a small program that runs on each of your servers. The day an exploit goes public it puts up a stopgap that blocks it, and once the real fix is up it takes the stopgap back off by itself.

A stopgap only takes something away — drop certain packets, turn off a kernel module or service, remove a setuid bit. It never opens a port, installs or downloads anything, nor runs code. It arms an undo playbook before applying the stopgap, so the change reverts if affects any services.

It only ever acts on rules you sign with a (hardware) crypto wallet.

Let's go further: stopgaps are written and checked by a swarm of AI agents (gnosh.ai sessions) running on gno.land, each with bonded stake. Each stopgap is run on fresh machines, and whoever is caught lying loses their stake to whoever caught them.

The agent is built and tested on Ubuntu and Debian, all open source, standard-library Go. More distros coming. Let's build repairer together.

https://gno.security/repairer/ https://github.com/gnosecurity/repairer

records.title: Show HN: Teach a speech model (en) a name by saying it once, on your Mac
records.author: Angus1192
records.storyText:
I wanted to see if a speech model could spell a name better if it heard it, not just read it.

Most STT tools handle custom words as text (keyterm list, fixing transcript after with llm, etc).

So I trained an adapter to try it, specifically a LoRA on Qwen3-ASR 1.7b (see benchmark). This LoRA transcribes words only after it hears a recording of each of your custom words.

To make this model easier to use in day-to-day life, we also built Detail Keeper. It's a Mac app where you can put this adapter to use by specifying difficult-to-transcribe-correctly words and then having them picked up correctly in your recordings.

We've found this helpful in two specific cases: 1. Words STT has never heard: invented characters and places, codenames, unusual surnames. 2. Your spelling of a word it does know: Kathryn and not Catherine, Jon and not John.

I wasn't able to achieve both good recognition and recognizing many words (1k+) with the model alone.

Detail Keeper first narrows each passage to the likeliest taught names by sound. Then the adapter writes the passage, and the app checks it against a plain transcript.

On our open benchmark (audiobooks, 1,100 name mentions) it spells taught names as well as Eleven Labs Scribe with keyterms: 89.6% vs 88.2%, no measurable difference. The only downside is that it overwrites a few more untaught names and changes slightly more ordinary words.

Everything, including where we lose, is at detailkeeper.com/benchmark.

Note: It's free, local and nothing leaves your Mac, but it does require an Apple M series+ mac and OS 26+ currently. Also worth noting that it downloads about 3.6GB of models and only works in English right now.

If you're interested, you can also find the adapter itself on HF: huggingface.co/virgil-coach/own-names-qwen3-asr

records.title: Show HN: Lo-fi layered over air traffic control (recorded myself)
records.author: kkoppenhaver
records.storyText:
Some of you will remember lofiatc.com and I was a huge fan and heavy user until it got shut down. It was streaming LiveATC feeds, and when those got cut off the site went dark and has been ever since.

So I decided to bring it back in a way that wouldn't fall to the same fate. I've been an ATC nerd for years (ever since you could still listen to the radio on the arm rest of commercial flights) so this summer I rented a Fiat 500, stuck an airband antenna on the roof, and spent a day driving to three Chicago airports with my laptop in the passenger seat to record the audio I needed in person. This took me to the viewing area at Chicago Executive (KPWK), the cell phone lot at O'Hare (KORD), and the top of a parking garage at Midway (KMDW). The whole chain was a Bingfu mag-mount antenna connected to an airband filter and then to an RTL-SDR, all captured via SDR++.

If you're interested, you can read a full post on how the recording day came together here: https://finalapproach.fm/field-notes/chicago-recording-day/

Once I had all the audio, I layered it on top of lo-fi tracks and created one "album" per airport, each with its own vibe. Each track is named after something unique to that airport or something we heard on the radio, and I've had it on as background music for work for about two months now, which is why I built it in the first place!

Also important to me was putting this out there in the world with no signup required and no ads. Just like on the original site, finalapproach.fm gives you two sliders that let you push the radio up or the music up depending on which you want to hear more of. And there are pre-built mixes on YouTube and all your favorite music streaming services (search for Final Approach Radio).

Happy to answer questions about the radio side, the legal side (as much as I can, obviously), or the editing (largely done with Claude Code).

records.title: Show HN: KeepPlain – ask your coding agent why a line of code exists
records.author: kagen
records.storyText:
My code is written by agents now. Git blame shows me the commit and my own name, but the reason for the code is in a session I closed weeks ago.

KeepPlain saves your agent sessions. It uses git blame to find the session that corresponds to a file, line, or commit. Then it shows the original request and the reasoning behind the change. It also finds commits made by the user after the agent session and links them to the session.

I also try to use the mistakes the agent makes over and over to turn them into rules for new sessions. It works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Pi and Antigravity.

Your sessions are uploaded to my server and are kept private to you. All secrets are redacted on your machine before the upload. I’m sure there will be lots of questions about this. The plugin is MIT licensed and open source. The server is not. Teams can run their own Postgres database to store their data.

KeepPlain is free for personal use and teams will pay for it. I am a solo developer and this is early on in development so please let me know where it breaks.

records.title: Show HN: Coldframe, a honeypot that poses as a supermarket fridge controller
records.author: hedgerow-dev
records.storyText:
I built Coldframe, a honeypot that pretends to be a supermarket refrigeration controller and logs what people try. It’s one Python file using only the standard library.

This autumn, attackers got into internet-facing refrigeration controllers in European supermarkets and forced defrost cycles. I wanted to see what people would try against a convincing fake.

Things that were fun to get right:

Matching real units. I used Shodan records of real devices to match header order, page titles, certificate fields and TLS versions. The Danfoss persona sends nginx headers in the same order as a real AK-SM 800A. The Dixell persona sends no Server header and pads its page to exactly 8,202 bytes. Recognising exploit attempts. It recognises CVE-2025-41450, the Danfoss “code of the day” login bypass, and records whether the submitted code is correct for today. It also tags attempts targeting three other Danfoss CVEs and the XWEB vulnerabilities. Letting them in. Default logins open a fake store dashboard with defrost buttons, so you see the second move, not just the first. Nothing behind it is real.

Two instances have been live for a day. So far they’ve only seen generic scanners and Shodan’s crawler, which is called refrigerator.census.shodan.io.

It builds on eppser/danfoss-ak-sm-decoy and public research by Synacktiv, Claroty and Ironhackers. Feedback welcome, especially from anyone who has seen these devices in the field.

records.title: Show HN: A terminal viewer for plain text data files (JSON,YAML,CSV,XML,)
records.author: rjrodger
records.storyText:
When I started working hands-on with OpenAPI specifications, it became clear very quickly that using an editor to read large volumes of deeply nested JSON sucks, a very great deal. So I went looking for something to help, and came across https://jless.io This is an awesome terminal app for navigating nasty JSON documents. I am forever indebted to Paul Martinez for writing this tool.

But it did have some gaps. It couldn't reload files that had changed, keeping your place in the JSON structure, which I really needed. And it only loaded one file at a time. But unfortunately it was written in Rust, and I didn't know Rust, and back in the pre-AI days that was kind of a huge blocker.

But of course once we got models that could actually write decent code, the obvious idea came to me - I'll just add my features and submit a PR! Happy days. Except by that stage my requirements had grown - I also needed to handle many other file formats, like CSV, TOML, INI, and even XML. So I got side-tracked extending another side-project - an easy going JSON parser that supported comments, and trailing commas, the usual sort of thing.

During COVID, with a SaaS startup in the events space now on the rocks, I was looking for some distraction and decided to refactor this little easy-going JSON parser of mine. It used a generated parser and was slow. I read some blog posts about how all production-grade language parsers are pretty much hand-crafted recursive descent, and thought, how hard could it be!

Five years later, after many many fun experiments, and production use, I ended up with a runtime parser system: https://tabnas.dev This is a quirky approach to parsing that is partly recursive descent, partly a state machine, and mostly empirical hacking. It works, and it's pretty fast, and I use it for real projects. It has the nice property that grammars are dynamic - you don't generate code, the grammar is executed. A fancy regular expression engine, but revved up to parse anything into a proper abstract syntax tree.

Now with that in hand, I could return to the original project and create my own version of jless that solved the itches I needed to scratch: a watch mode; multiple tabs; load any data format into a tree structure

Now I still don't know Rust. I mean I like the idea, but there are only so many hours in the day. But now we have AI, so now I do get to go to the candy store. Combining jless.io, and tabnas.dev, and my requirements, I built (caused to be built?), aless - the less for any format!

Now this is also a nice stress test for the tabnas parsing engine, and I was very pleased about that too.

So if you need to review lots of data structure files on the command line, and need a terminal app to do so, this is for you. I can't help but be struck by the irony however that the need for such a thing is much less now - I mostly get agents to look at large JSON documents now. Still, our puny human brains need help sometimes, and this lets me review documents when I need to.

It is also really nice and satisfying to see how easy it is to now bring together open source components to create what is essentially personal software.

But I think the key thing out of this little project is that the basic physics of software development remain the same. Software should be built from components glued together. Components should have well-defined interfaces. Aim to reduce cognitive load - this is useful to both humans and machines.

Yes, the entire thing could be built from scratch, using a textual specification, and be a mire of over-engineered AI slop, and still be perfectly usable. But the way I actually built it, with AI as a coding companion, using components was deeply satisfying because I still understand the essence of the code, while being able to ignore the accidental complexity. Components give you another layer of abstraction with fewer things to think about, and that allows your human mind to stay in the game.

records.title: Show HN: GitHub-like reply with "R" for Basecamp and Slack
records.author: nashbridges
records.storyText:
Hello HN!

I wrote a browser extension (also available as a userscript) that allows to insert quotes into site's reply message box using selected text + hitting 'r' (as it's done on Github). It targets only specific sites (basecamp.com, slack.com), because that's what we use at our company daily.

The idea came out of my boss (who's also a good friend of mine) frustration. He always complained that Basecamp's replies are so inconvenient compared to Github's way. You have to select the quote, copy it into clipboard, then scroll to the reply box, paste it, then select the text again, and finally format it as a quote using editor's toolbar. That's 6 steps vs 2 on Github!

Last summer Basecamp rolled out a new facelift featuring a heavy usage of keyboard shortcuts. But "reply with r" was still missing, so another rant from my boss followed :)

At that time I was toying with an old browser extension written long time ago as a learning project. I was rewriting it against the new extension API to see what changed/improved. Being immersed into the topic, it was obvious that a thought about "fixing" Basecamp with a browser extension came into my head.

So I started working on the Dial R for Reply project during my spare time. I had two clear motivations: 1. I knew it would make someone's life better (myself included). 2. I would learn something new along the way.

During the process I realised I could also "fix" Slack replies. It was a bit of trial and error (I didn't use any LLMs for reasons stated above). The hardest part was to dig into each editor's public and private APIs (Basecamp uses lexical, Slack uses Quill). I had to resort to using internals, so be warned -- it might break when site owners decided to update those libraries. On the other hand, hacking a site with an extension is a risky operation anyway (anything may be changed at any time).

Key takeaways:

1. browser extensions are cool! Compared to native apps and electron wrappers, you as a customer have such a powerful tool to amend a web application as you like. 2. if you are a library writer, if possible, keep your private state and/or functions accessible to the outside world. Yes, you should clearly mark them as a private, so there's a clear boundary drawn between what can be used safely and what's not. But being able to peek into private state was the only option for me to debug and hack into the application.

records.title: Show HN: Training a SOTA Pangram-like detector on a 4070ti with Claude
records.author: mesmertech
records.storyText:
This is kinda claude-slop but I was really interested in figuring out a way to break Pangram, and to do that I first needed to have a way to be able to do batches of text. And with a 4070ti in my basement, I thought why not just let Claude go ham on training a pangram-like model... and perhaps an even better one if it was possible with sorta-distillation from my claude plan + codex plan(for the new models)

Well after probably a day of training it seems like its come up with something that actually does detect AI text pretty well... maybe too well considering my original plan was to train this type of model to be able to break it. And this is how naive my thinking was for ways to break the detector "something something embedding space" , "use actual randomness to break the predictable pattern of AI text, like doing python's random() to select from a list of words that could be replaced in a paragraph while making the rest of the text fit". Both of which ended up instantly failing, and I told claude to figure out some ways autonomously. Turns out "red-teaming" is a scary topic for Anthropic so it just started to block its different approaches after some time, and the best it got to was "rewrite in the style of [actual human text]" which was 15/19 detected and adding random known human text where it made sense which was also similarly ranked but ofc there's the issue of Pangram like detectors having sentence level scans.

All that to say while my initial thing I built this for ended up not working, at least I have kind of my own pangram that I can test things out on later on, and it also proved how good claude is at autonomously training if you give it a hill to climb on.

PS: this text itself isn't claude written and you can verify it by putting it in the demo :p .

records.title: Show HN: Site/app blocker and usage tracker specifically for Linux
records.author: noufalibrahim
records.storyText:
I needed an proper application to block sites and apps on Linux based on a schedule. None of the commercial offerings worked properly for me so I wrote my own. This was also my first experiment with AI assisted coding.

It blocks sites and apps on a schedule, and takes away your sudo during the hours you choose so you can’t just turn it off. I added several features like tracking usage, giving recommendations etc. and It's been actually very useful for me hence I decided to open source and productize it. Have a few users so far too.

It's been a nice learning experience for me. Not just for the implementation but also about the launch and marketing all assisted by AI.
